extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, educators, researchers and policymakers interested in misinformation and media manipulation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and background on what constitutes a fake news website, the methods they use, how they spread, notable examples, and responses (educational, commercial, governmental) in the U.S. context. Useful for people seeking criteria to identify or study fake-news sites and countermeasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of fake news websites
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news websites deliberately publish hoaxes, propaganda, and disinformation to drive web traffic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These sites are distinguished from news satire because fake news articles are usually fabricated to deliberately mislead readers, either for profit or disinformation campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from satire
rubrics_metrics.description: News satire traditionally signals itself as satire, whereas fake news fabricates stories to mislead; satire can still deceive readers if not clearly labeled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire sites have received criticism for not properly notifying readers that they are publishing false or satirical content, since many readers have been duped by seemingly legitimate articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clickbait headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary or incredible article titles designed to entice users to click, often withholding significant information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clickbait often leads to exaggerated or fake titles; Facebook defines clickbait as headlines that withhold significant amounts of information and mislead the user. Extraordinary story titles played a large part in tricking users who cannot tell if the article is real.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of manipulated or out-of-context images
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting inflammatory, manipulated, or out-of-context images to make articles appear legitimate or more shocking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manipulated images can cause readers to incorrectly assume legitimacy, often due to their inflammatory image choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impersonation of legitimate news organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Copying formatting, names, and appearances of real news organizations to trick readers into believing a site is legitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impersonation can be crude (spoofing an organization's name/format) or exact copies that closely mimic a legitimate outlet's site and staff listings; exact copies can trick viewers into believing the website is an official organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typosquatting and domain tricks
rubrics_metrics.description: Registering domains that rely on common misspellings, slight rephrasings, or uncommon top-level domains (e.g., .com.co) to catch accidental traffic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typosquatters monitor clicks to 'typo' domains and sell advertising; many fake sites exploited misspellings and alternate TLDs to appear like legitimate publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscurity and lack of attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake sites often omit author identities, have no About Us page, or invent reporter identities, reducing transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since authors are not actual reporters, many fake news sites pretend to have a reporter identity or simply do not include author/about information; being publicized by real organizations can lend them undue legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authoring style that mixes plausible top with absurd detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing that appears legitimate at the top of an article but becomes increasingly absurd as the reader progresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some fake-news writers intentionally craft articles that seem credible early on and insert absurd, fabricated details later to both draw clicks and evade cursory checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivations: economic (ad revenue) vs ideological
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news is produced either to gain viewers and ad revenue or to advance ideological/disinformation campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include teenage operators earning ad revenue and site operators claiming political motives; both economic and ideological drivers shape content and distribution strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media amplification and algorithmic factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news spreads via social platforms and can be amplified by algorithms and sharing behavior, sometimes outperforming real news in engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research showed fake stories receiving massive attention on Facebook and Twitter; platform algorithms and user sharing (including virality from single influential shares) play central roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virality metrics as indicators of spread
rubrics_metrics.description: High counts of shares, reactions, and comments on social platforms indicate rapid spread and potential impact of fake news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistics cited include top fake stories having more combined engagement than top real-news stories (e.g., millions of shares/reactions/comments). Sudden spikes in search rankings for false claims also indicate spread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of AI-generated images/photographs in campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Actors have used photos generated with artificial intelligence to create inauthentic accounts and avoid simple detection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the 2020 cycle, networks used AI-generated images to help fake accounts appear authentic, complicating platform detection efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public and student difficulties in identifying fake content
rubrics_metrics.description: Many people, including students, struggle to differentiate advertisements from news articles and to identify source credibility markers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Stanford study found middle/high/college students had trouble discerning ads from news and only a minority recognized verification badges; graphic elements can mislead readers into trusting fake accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational countermeasures (classroom techniques)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching strategies (e.g., fake-news challenges, rapid true/false assessments) help students practice discerning true vs false news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: teachers having students read articles and decide truthfulness under time pressure; classes writing fake articles to test peers' detection skills; OECD proposals to test 'global competencies' including discerning fake news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform/commercial countermeasures (Facebook example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms can flag disputed stories, demote content failing fact-checks, reduce financial incentives, hire content reviewers, and work with third-party fact-checkers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facebook announced flagging mechanisms where user reports send stories to third-party organizations; failed items lose news feed priority and receive 'disputed by 3rd party fact-checkers' captions. Platforms also seek to reduce ad revenue incentives and hire thousands of content reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of fact-checking organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent fact-checkers (e.g., Snopes, PolitiFact, FactCheck.org) investigate claims, publish lists/guides of fake sites, and collaborate with platforms to assess veracity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the 2016 election, many fact-checkers teamed with Facebook; fact-checking orgs also maintain lists and guides to identify fake news websites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governmental and legislative responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative bodies investigate foreign influence, hold hearings, request intelligence declassification, and pass measures funding counter-propaganda efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include U.S. Senate Intelligence Committee hearings on Russian operations, the Countering Foreign Propaganda and Disinformation Act authorizing funding, and bipartisan calls to track and counter alleged propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: FTC and enforcement against deceptive commercial schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators like the Federal Trade Commission can take enforcement action when fake-news sites are used to deceive consumers for commercial gain (e.g., bogus health claims tied to fake news sites).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FTC charged operators who used fake news websites to promote products and obtained monetary settlements; consumer-deception frameworks can apply to fake-news-based fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counter-Disinformation organizational efforts and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Government-created units (e.g., Counter-Disinformation Team) can be formed to combat propaganda but may be disbanded or constrained by policy choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The U.S. State Department planned a Counter-Disinformation Team to combat Russian propaganda but canceled it after department leadership missed the scope of propaganda prior to the 2016 election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lists of notable fake-news sites as indicators/examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific sites (e.g., ABCnews.com.co, Denver Guardian, National Report, News Examiner) exemplify tactics like impersonation, clickbait, and monetization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examining such examples can reveal concrete tactics: ABCnews.com.co spoofed ABC News; Denver Guardian ran a fabricated viral story; some operators reported earnings from ad revenue tied to fake election stories.
